title: Longest Common Prefix
directAnswer: Find the longest string that is a prefix of every string in the array. The cleanest answer is vertical scanning: walk column 0, 1, 2… of the first string and check that same column matches in every other string; stop at the first mismatch or the first string that runs out. O(S) time where S is the total number of characters.

rules: **Handle the empty array first.** `strs = []` must return `""` — dereferencing `strs[0]` without this guard throws.
**Stop the moment a string runs out.** When the column index `i` equals some string's length, the prefix can't grow past `i` — return `strs[0][0..i]`.
**The answer can never be longer than the shortest string.** That's the loop bound and the key invariant.
**A single empty string in the array forces the answer to `""`.** `["", "abc"]` → `""`, because column 0 already runs out.
**Compare against the first string, not a running buffer you rebuild.** Slicing `strs[0]` once at the end is cheaper and clearer than appending char by char.
whenToUse: You need the shared leading characters across a set of strings
The match must be a true prefix — anchored at index 0, not a substring anywhere
Autocomplete / routing / file-path collapsing where common roots matter
Input is a list of strings and order doesn't matter to the answer
antiSignals: Need the longest common *substring* (anywhere) → DP or suffix structures, not a prefix scan
Matching one pattern against many strings repeatedly → build a Trie instead
Only two strings and you want suffix overlap → that's a different (Z/KMP) problem
remember.takeaway: Longest Common Prefix is the gentlest 'compare strings column by column' problem. Vertical scanning is the interview-grade answer; the binary-search and divide-and-conquer variants are nice to *name* but rarely worth coding unless asked. The real skill being tested is careful boundary handling: empty array, empty string, and the shorter-string cutoff.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you handle the messy edge cases (empty array, empty string, single string) cleanly and pick a simple linear scan instead of over-engineering — and whether you can articulate why the answer is bounded by the shortest string.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Dereferencing `strs[0]` before checking the array is non-empty, or looping past the end of a shorter string and throwing an index error.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the shortest-string bound up front, write the clean vertical scan, then mention that binary search on the prefix length (O(S log m)) and divide-and-conquer exist as alternatives — without claiming they beat O(S).

problemStatement:
Write a function to find the longest common prefix string amongst an array of strings `strs`.

If there is no common prefix, return an empty string `""`.

A *prefix* must be anchored at the start of every string — `"fl"` is a prefix of `"flower"`, but `"low"` is not.
constraints: strs[i] consists of only lowercase English letters
An individual string may be empty (length 0)
understanding: Return the longest string that appears, unchanged, at the front of every input string. The answer length is at most the length of the shortest string, and a single empty string in the input collapses the answer to "".

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array itself be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: By the constraints it has at least one element, but I'll still guard `strs.length == 0 → ""` so the code is robust if reused elsewhere.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can an individual string be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. `["", "abc"]` returns `""` because the empty string has no column 0 to match.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is matching case-sensitive?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The constraints say lowercase only, so it doesn't matter here — but I'd confirm, since `"Flower"` vs `"flower"` would otherwise differ at column 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the prefix have to be anchored at the start?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — prefix means index 0 onward. A shared substring elsewhere doesn't count; that's a different, harder problem.

examples.explanation: Columns 0 ('f') and 1 ('l') match everywhere; column 2 is 'o','o','i' → mismatch, so we stop at length 2.
Column 0 is 'd','r','c' — they disagree immediately, so there is no common prefix.
The first string is empty, so the loop bound is 0 and we return "" without comparing anything.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Decide what kind of 'common' you need before writing code. LCP is the prefix-anchored, scan-by-column branch.

approaches.name: Vertical Scanning (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this — it's the cleanest answer and naturally handles the shorter-string cutoff. Phrase it as 'check one column across all strings, top to bottom'.
hints: The answer can never be longer than the shortest string — so you only ever look at columns 0 through (shortest length − 1). What do all strings have to agree on at each column?
Fix a column index i. Take the character at position i in the first string, then check every other string has the same character at position i. The first column that fails ends the prefix.
Two ways a column fails: some string is too short to have an index i at all, or it has a different character there. Both mean 'stop and return strs[0] up to i'.
approaches.complexityReasoning: In the worst case (all strings identical) we touch every character once: S = sum of all lengths. No buffer is built, so extra space is O(1) beyond the output.
approaches.explanation:
Picture the strings stacked on top of each other, aligned at the left edge, like rows in a table. The longest common prefix is the widest block of fully-matching **columns** starting from column 0. Vertical scanning walks those columns left to right and stops at the first one that isn't unanimous.

**Why we anchor on `strs[0]`.** The prefix, if it exists, is a prefix of *every* string — including the first one. So `strs[0]` is a perfectly good reference: its character at column `i` is the candidate, and we only need to verify the *other* strings agree. There's no need to maintain a separate growing buffer; we just remember how far we got and slice `strs[0]` once at the end.

**The two ways a column dies.** For column `i`, a string `s` breaks the prefix in exactly two situations: either `i == len(s)` — `s` simply ran out of characters and can't extend the prefix any further — or `s[i] != c` — `s` has a character here but it's the wrong one. Folding both into a single `if (i == len(s) || s[i] != c)` is what makes the inner loop both correct and tidy. The `i == len(s)` half is precisely the shorter-string cutoff, handled for free without computing the minimum length up front.

**Why this is the answer interviewers want.** It's `O(S)` — you can't do better than reading the shared characters at least once — it uses `O(1)` extra space, and it makes the edge cases obvious rather than hidden. The empty-array guard is the only ceremony; after that, an empty string in the input ends the scan at column 0 automatically, and a single-element array returns that element unchanged. Simple, linear, and boundary-safe.
approaches.insight: The shorter-string cutoff and the character-mismatch are the *same* event — 'this column is not unanimous' — so they belong in one condition. Candidates who write a separate `Math.min` length pre-pass aren't wrong, but the `i == len(s)` check inside the loop is strictly cleaner and proves you understand the invariant.

diagrams.title: Why a column dies
diagrams.caption: Each column must be unanimous. The scan ends at the first column that isn't — either a mismatch or a string that ran out.

edgeCases.behavior: len(strs[0]) is 0, so the outer loop body never runs → return "" (the whole first string).
Only one string; the inner loop never runs, every column passes → return "abc".
At i=2, i == len("ab") triggers the shorter-string cutoff → return "ab".

pitfalls: Indexing strs[0] before the empty-array guard — throws on strs = [].
Testing s[i] before i == len(s) — raises IndexError / StringIndexOutOfBounds on a shorter string.
Returning strs[0].substring(0, i+1) instead of (0, i) — off-by-one that includes the failing column.

approaches.name: Binary Search on Prefix Length (Alternative)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention as a 'we could also' if asked for alternatives — it's clever but not asymptotically better in practice. Pair it with naming divide-and-conquer.
hints: The set of valid prefix lengths is monotonic: if a prefix of length L is common to all strings, then so is every shorter length. That monotonic boundary is exactly what binary search exploits.
Let m be the shortest string's length. Binary search the largest L in [0, m] such that strs[0][0:L] is a prefix of every string.
For a candidate length mid, checking 'is this a common prefix?' costs O(n·mid). Wrap that in a binary search over L to get O(S log m).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each isCommonPrefix check scans up to n strings × mid chars = O(S). We do O(log m) such checks, giving O(S log m). No extra structures → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
This approach reframes the problem as a search over **the answer's length** rather than a scan over characters. The key observation is monotonicity: if all strings share a prefix of length `L`, they automatically share every prefix shorter than `L`; and if they fail to share a prefix of length `L`, they fail every longer one too. That yes-then-no boundary is the classic setup for binary search.

**How the search runs.** We bound the answer to `[0, m]` where `m` is the shortest string's length — nothing longer can be common. We binary search the largest `mid` for which `strs[0][0:mid]` is a prefix of *all* strings. If `mid` works, the answer is at least `mid`, so we move the low bound up; if it fails, the answer is below `mid`, so we drop the high bound. We use the `(lo + hi + 1) / 2` midpoint to bias upward and avoid an infinite loop when `lo` and `hi` are adjacent.

**Why it isn't actually faster.** The per-check cost is `O(S)` and we run `O(log m)` checks, so the total is `O(S log m)` — *worse* than the vertical scan's `O(S)` by a logarithmic factor. The win, if any, is when the common prefix is short and strings are long: binary search may bail after touching fewer characters on average. But the worst case is genuinely slower, so present this as a discussion point, not an upgrade.

**The cousin: divide-and-conquer.** A third option splits the array in half, recursively computes the LCP of each half, and merges by taking the common prefix of the two results. It's also `O(S)` total and parallelizes nicely, but for an interview it's strictly more code than the vertical scan for the same big-O. Naming both binary search and divide-and-conquer signals breadth; coding the vertical scan signals judgment.
approaches.insight: The unlock is recognizing that 'valid prefix lengths' form a monotonic predicate (true, true, …, true, false, …, false). Any time a property flips exactly once along an axis, binary search the flip point — that mental trigger is far more reusable than this specific problem.

dryRun.intro: Shortest length m = 4 ("flow"). Binary search the largest L in [0, 4] that is a common prefix length.

mid works → the answer is at least mid; keep mid in the feasible range.
One disagreeing string is enough to reject this candidate length.

python.explanation: Upper bound of the search — nothing longer than the shortest string can be common.
Upper-biased midpoint prevents an infinite loop when lo and hi are adjacent.

edgeCases.behavior: min_len = 0 → hi = 0, loop never runs → return "".

pitfalls: Using (lo + hi) / 2 with the lo = mid update — infinite loop when hi = lo + 1.
Forgetting the empty-array / empty-string guard, so min_len or substring(0, len) misbehaves.
Claiming this beats the vertical scan — it's O(S log m), strictly worse in the worst case.

commonMistakes: Accessing strs[0] before checking the array is non-empty.
Reading s[i] before confirming i < len(s), throwing on a shorter string.
Treating 'prefix' as 'substring anywhere' and trying to match in the middle of strings.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: No empty-array guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Every solution dereferences strs[0]. With strs = [], that throws ArrayIndexOutOfBounds (Java) or IndexError (Python) before any logic runs.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Indexing a shorter string out of bounds
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Checking the character before the length means a string that is shorter than the current column index throws instead of cleanly ending the prefix.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Off-by-one in the returned slice
commonMistakesDetailed.why: i is the first column that FAILED, so the agreed prefix is [0, i). Slicing to i+1 sneaks the failing column into the answer.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return strs[0].substring(0, i + 1); // includes the mismatching column
commonMistakesDetailed.good: return strs[0].substring(0, i);     // excludes the column that failed

patternNote: Vertical character agreement across multiple strings. The same column-by-column thinking shows up in any 'what do all these strings share at the front?' task, and the Trie generalizes it when you need repeated prefix queries. Binary-search-on-answer and divide-and-conquer are reusable templates worth recognizing even though the linear scan wins here.
